extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (readers of a logic textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature of names and propositions, the distinction between verbal (essential) and real (accidental) propositions, and the theory of classification (the five predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens). Guidance on what counts as a real 'Kind' versus an accidental class and how propositions function in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real and Nominal Essences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes nominal essences (essences of classes, i.e., connotations of names) from real essences (supposed causes of sensible properties of individual objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominal essences explain the connotation of class-names; real essences, if known, would allow demonstration of sensible properties from them alone. The author notes Locke's admission that real essences are unknown, which makes the fiction comparatively innocuous; in physics 'real essence' of bodies comes to be conceived as nearly equivalent to corpuscular structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential (Verbal) Propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: An essential proposition is purely verbal: it asserts of a thing under a particular name only what is asserted by the fact of calling it by that name; it gives no information about the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such propositions either give no information or give it regarding the name rather than the thing; they are not instructive and stand on a level with their premises. The author avoids using essential propositions as examples except where specifically required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essential (Accidental or Real) Propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that predicate of a thing some fact not involved in the signification of the name; they convey information not already involved in the meanings of the words and thus, if true, add to our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These include propositions about individually designated things and general/particular propositions where the predicate connotes an attribute not connoted by the subject. Only this class is intrinsically instructive or can yield instructive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Essential Propositions as Teaching Examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Using examples that are purely essential (verbal) makes logic appear futile because such examples prove nothing beyond the meaning of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author 'studiously avoided the employment of essential propositions as examples' in order to illustrate logical doctrines with propositions that provide genuine information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Aspects of General Propositions: Speculative vs Practical (Memoranda)
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions can be viewed either as portions of speculative/theoretical truth or as memoranda for practical use (indicating what to expect in individual cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative form: 'All men are mortal' as an expression of attributes that are always accompanied by mortality. Practical/memorandum form: the attributes of man are marks or evidence of mortality. For reasoning, the practical/mark/evidence formulation is often more useful because it suggests how propositions are applied to derive others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional View of Propositions in Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: In reasoning, propositions enter as means to establish other propositions rather than as ultimate results; best viewed as asserting that one fact or phenomenon is a mark or evidence of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends defining the import of a proposition in the mode that most distinctly suggests its use in advancing from it to other propositions — i.e., as evidence/marks — because this highlights their role in the theory of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How Classification Arises from General Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Every general name that connote attributes potentially creates a class constituted by things possessing those attributes; whether actual objects exist is immaterial to the signification of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names may be introduced primarily to express a signification (predication) or to create a class for convenience (classification). The names of scientific classes (e.g., Cuvier's) are as much expressions of attributes as other connotative names; the peculiarity is whether classification motivated introduction of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Five Predicables
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of general names into five predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distinctions are not grounded upon differences in meaning (attributes connoted) but upon differences in the kind of class they denote — i.e., the relation the predicate bears to the subject in a given classification. The same name may serve as genus, species, or differentia depending on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus and Species as Relative Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus and species indicate relations between predicate and subject: a term may be a genus with respect to one subject and a species with respect to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'animal' is genus relative to 'man', but species relative to 'substance' or 'being'; 'rectangular' is a differentia for a square but an accident for a table. Therefore, genus/species status depends on classification context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian Restriction: Genus and Species Must Be of the Essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotelian logicians restricted genus and species to those classes considered 'of the essence' of the subject; not every class that can be divided or included is admitted as genus/species under this view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this view, a genus/species must be a 'Kind' in a deeper sense — an indeterminate/inexhaustible set of properties — whereas superficial divisions (e.g., biped for man) would be classed as proprium or accidens and not granted genus/species status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Meaning of Genus/Species as Real Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A real Kind (genus or species in the logical sense) is a class distinguished from other classes by an indeterminate multitude of properties not derivable from one another; such kinds are the only classes the Aristotelians admitted as true genera or species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes 'natural' or 'radical' classifications (where members share many, possibly unknown, common properties) from arbitrary or convenience-based classes (e.g., color classes) whose commonalities are finite and determinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited Power to Frame Classes and the Criterion for Naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic allows framing classes on any attribute (if some have it and others do not), so the number of possible classes is boundless; but some classes differ from others only by finite enumerables of properties while others by multitudinous/indefinite properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classes whose members differ from non-members by an inexhaustible set of properties (e.g., animals, plants) answer to more 'radical' distinctions (natural Kinds); classes based only on finite/determinate properties (white, black) are less 'natural' and may be disregarded unless required by purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate (Infima) Species and Inclusion of Properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate (lowest) Kind to which an individual is referable (its species) comprises properties that necessarily include all common properties of any other real Kind to which the individual belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the proximate Kind is ascertained, every other Kind predicable of the individual will stand in the relation of genus to that proximate Kind; this explains the logical meaning of genus and species in a classificatory hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia: Distinguishing Attributes and the 'Essence' Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentia is the attribute (or set of attributes) that distinguishes a species from every other species of the same genus; the Aristotelians required the differentia to be of the essence of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author highlights a problem: species are distinguished by an indefinite number of properties, so singling out one as the differentia (and requiring it be 'essential') is problematic. Differentiae may be more than one attribute and the Aristotelian demand that it be of essence is questioned as obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for When a Class Counts as a 'Kind' (vs Accident)
rubrics_metrics.description: A class counts as a real Kind (a 'logical species') when the differences separating it from other classes extend to an indefinite/inexhaustible series of properties (known and unknown), not merely to a determinate finite set of attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If differences between groups can be traced to a few primary differences under laws of nature, they are not distinct Kinds in the logician's sense; if not traceable, they may be legitimately ranked as different species by the logician even if naturalists would not.
